title: The Northern Sky

narrative.text: The situation room smells like burnt coffee and recirculated air. Dusek is at the map before you enter. She doesn't turn around.
Northern border. Three aircraft. Turned back forty minutes ago.
She traces a line on the map with one finger. The line goes twelve kilometers inside Veltrian airspace before it turns back.
This one held position for eleven minutes.
She taps a point on the map. Directly above the Dravenhollow communications relay.
They wanted us to see them.
Vyktor and Theron arrive together. Neither of them has slept.

monologue: Three aircraft. Twelve kilometers inside our airspace. Eleven minutes above a communications relay. Dusek is right — this was not accidental navigation. Someone in Tyvaren wanted us to count them. The question is what they wanted the counting to mean. A test of our response time. A message about our vulnerability. Or something else entirely — a provocation designed to make us do something they can point to.

choices.text: What are we looking at in terms of Tyvaren capability? What can they actually do?
Why now? What's changed in Tyvaren that makes this the week they test us?
Dusek — what do you recommend?
Theron — has Tyvaren done this before? What happened?

dialogue.text: Tyvaren operates a modern air force — primarily Confederation-supplied equipment. Their northern wing has approximately sixty combat-capable aircraft within range of our border. We have forty-two, eight of which are in maintenance rotation.
In a direct engagement, we are at a disadvantage. That is not the relevant calculation. The relevant calculation is whether they want an engagement or a concession.
The Confederation won't sanction direct military action against Veltria. Tyvaren knows this. So do we. Which means this is about something other than military advantage.

choices.text: Then what is it about?
What are our response options?

dialogue.text: Three things changed in the last thirty days. Your government was sworn in — Tyvaren watched the election and did not like the result. The Arcturian Commonwealth made an overture to Veltria that became public — Tyvaren read that as a signal you might move east. And the Morivask situation is deteriorating in ways that affect the northern trade routes Tyvaren depends on.
They are anxious. Anxious powers do one of two things — they negotiate or they probe. This is a probe. They want to know what you'll do before they decide which path to take.
What we do in the next seventy-two hours tells them everything they need to know about this government's spine.

choices.text: Dusek — given that framing, what do you recommend?
What are our actual options?

dialogue.text: Stand down.
Silence. Vyktor looks up. Theron stops writing.
We scramble interceptors, we have a provocation. We have a provocation, we have a response. We have a response, we have an escalation. I have seen where that road ends, Chancellor.
A pause. When she continues her voice is exactly the same.
It ends in fields.
File a formal protest through diplomatic channels. Demand an explanation. Make the record. But do not give them the incident they came here looking for.
She does not say where she has seen this before. She does not explain what she means by fields. She waits for orders.

choices.text: I hear you. What does a diplomatic protest actually accomplish?
Standing down completely — doesn't that confirm their read that we won't respond?
Show me all the options.

dialogue.text: There is a difference between not scrambling interceptors and not responding. A diplomatic protest is a response. A public statement is a response. Requesting an emergency session of the Asturien Forum is a response. None of them give Tyvaren the military incident they can use to justify whatever comes next.

History suggests that restraint in these situations reads as either wisdom or weakness depending entirely on what follows. The question isn't what we do now — it's what we demonstrate we're prepared to do if it happens again.
I note that I have been wrong before.

choices.text: Give me the full options.
I've heard enough.

dialogue.text: 1947. Tyvaren conducted similar airspace incursions during the transition between the provisional government and the first elected chancellor. That chancellor scrambled interceptors. Tyvaren protested to the Asturien Forum. The Forum censured Veltria for escalation. It was three years before the diplomatic relationship recovered.
1952. Similar incursion. That chancellor filed a formal protest and requested bilateral talks. Tyvaren agreed to talks and the incursions stopped for four years.
The historical record suggests the diplomatic response produces better outcomes. I offer this as data, not as a recommendation. The situation today has variables that 1947 and 1952 did not.

choices.text: Dusek — same question to you. What do you recommend?
Show me the current options.

dialogue.text: A formal protest creates a record. If this escalates, we can demonstrate we responded through proper channels first. The Asturien Forum will want that record. Our neighbors will want that record.
It also buys time. Tyvaren has to respond to a formal protest. That response tells us something about what they actually want.
While we wait for their response, I want to move two additional squadrons to Dravenhollow. Quietly. No announcement. Let them discover it when their satellites pass.

choices.text: I've heard enough. Here's my decision.

dialogue.text: Three options. Diplomatic protest only — file with the Tyvaren foreign ministry and the Asturien Forum, no military response, monitor for repetition. Intercept and escort — scramble two fighters, intercept the next incursion if it occurs, escort the aircraft out of our airspace without engagement. Or forward deployment — move additional squadrons to the northern bases, make the deployment visible, let Tyvaren recalculate.
There is a fourth option which I'll name and then recommend against. Do nothing officially. No protest, no deployment. See if it happens again.
That option historically has not produced favorable outcomes.
No. It hasn't.

choices.text: If we intercept — what's the risk of an incident?
Forward deployment — what signal does that send?
I've heard enough. My decision.

dialogue.text: Intercept and escort is a standard procedure with a defined protocol. The risk is that Tyvaren sends aircraft that do not follow the protocol. In that scenario our pilots have rules of engagement that authorize defensive action. Defensive action becomes an incident. An incident becomes whatever Tyvaren's government decides to make of it.
The risk is low if Tyvaren is probing. The risk is higher if Tyvaren is looking for a pretext.

choices.text: Understood. My decision.

dialogue.text: Forward deployment signals that the new government is not a transitional uncertainty — that we have a defense posture and we're prepared to maintain it. Tyvaren's calculation presumably included the assumption that a new government takes six months to establish its military position. Deployment contradicts that assumption.
It also costs money we haven't budgeted for and gives the press a story about military buildup that could complicate the constitutional reform message.

choices.text: I've heard it all. Here's what we're doing.

dialogue.text: The map is still on the table. The line Dusek drew — twelve kilometers, eleven minutes, directly above the communications relay — is still there.
Your orders, Chancellor.

final_tyvaren_choice.monologue: Three aircraft wanted us to count them. Dusek has seen where escalation ends. Theron has the historical record. Vyktor has the political calculation. And I have the map with a line drawn through our airspace by someone who wanted to know what we would do. The answer I give now is the answer they will use to decide what comes next.

choices.text: Diplomatic protest only. File with Tyvaren and the Asturien Forum. No military response. Monitor closely and respond to any repetition with escalating diplomatic measures.

reactions.text: I'll file the protest by morning. I'm moving two squadrons to Dravenhollow on my own authority as a routine rotation. No announcement.
The Arcturian ambassador will want a statement. I'll draft something measured.
The press will call it weak. The Assembly will call it prudent. Both are correct.

choices.text: Establish intercept policy. Next incursion, we scramble and escort out. No engagement unless they fire first. File the diplomatic protest simultaneously.

reactions.text: She picks up the phone before you finish speaking.
That will require a public explanation if it's exercised. I'll prepare language.
I'll brief the Assembly defense committee tomorrow morning.

choices.text: Forward deployment. Move two additional squadrons to Dravenhollow. Make it visible. File the diplomatic protest. Let them recalculate.

reactions.text: Deployment will be complete in seventy-two hours. Their satellites will see it by the end of the week.
The press story is now military buildup. I'll frame it as defensive posture review.
History suggests this either deters the next incursion or accelerates Tyvaren's timeline. I cannot tell you which.

choices.text: Request direct bilateral talks with Tyvaren. No military response. Propose a formal border security agreement. Turn their probe into a negotiation.

reactions.text: If they accept, it transforms the relationship entirely. If they decline, we have a very clear record of which side sought de-escalation.
While we wait for their response, I want those two squadrons moved north. Quietly.
The Arcturian Commonwealth will be watching how Tyvaren responds. This may be more useful to us than it appears.
